Regression tables for survey designs

Source: vignettes/articles/table-regression-survey.Rmd
table-regression-survey.Rmd
library(spicy)
library(survey) # svydesign(), svyglm(), svyolr(), svycoxph()

This article covers regression on data from a complex survey: models fitted with the survey package (Lumley, 2004) on a declared design, svyglm(), svyolr() and svycoxph(). The descriptive side of the same designs is in Summary tables from a survey design. The companion article Publication-ready regression tables covers the shared mechanics (output engines, labels, tidy()), and the class-by-class map is Supported models.

Why a design, and what it changes

A survey sample is rarely a simple random sample. Units are drawn with unequal probabilities, within strata, and often in clusters: schools within districts, households within census tracts. Design-based inference takes that selection mechanism as the source of randomness. In Binder’s words, “the probabilities used to select the sample are then used as the basis for statistical inference, and such inference refers back to the finite population from which the random sample was selected” (Binder, 2008, p. 191).

For a regression table, this has consequences in three places.

The coefficients solve weighted estimating equations. The estimator is a pseudo-maximum likelihood estimator (Binder, 1992, p. 141): it has the form of a likelihood equation, but the sample has no likelihood under the design. Everything that needs one is therefore missing, the likelihood-ratio test and the usual AIC first.

The variance comes from the design. Strata, clusters and a finite population correction all enter it, by linearization or by replicate weights. The weights alone do not determine it.

The reference distribution of the tests comes from the design too. Its degrees of freedom are counted on the primary sampling units, not on the rows.

Whether a regression should be weighted at all is a modelling question that no table settles. When the sampling is informative, model-based estimates “can be severely biased” (Binder, 2008, p. 193), and “the appropriateness of the weighted regression estimate depends on which model is chosen” (DuMouchel & Duncan, 1983, p. 535). This article starts after that decision: the analysis is design-based, and the question is how to report it.

The designs used here

The examples use the data that ship with survey. The api data hold the Academic Performance Index of Californian schools, with several samples of the same population: apiclus1 is a cluster sample of 15 school districts, apistrat a sample stratified by school type. The nhanes data are an extract of NHANES 2009-2010 on high cholesterol, with the strata, the primary sampling units and the examination weights of the survey.

data(api)
data(nhanes)

dclus1 <- svydesign(id = ~dnum, weights = ~pw, data = apiclus1, fpc = ~fpc)

nhanes$race <- factor(
  nhanes$race,
  levels = 1:4,
  labels = c("Hispanic", "White", "Black", "Other")
)
nhanes$sex <- factor(
  nhanes$RIAGENDR,
  levels = 1:2,
  labels = c("Male", "Female")
)
dnh <- svydesign(
  id = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTMEC2YR,
  nest = TRUE, data = nhanes
)
dnh
#> Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement)
#> With (31) clusters.
#> svydesign(id = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTMEC2YR, 
#>     nest = TRUE, data = nhanes)

A first table

A linear model of the school’s score in 2000 on three characteristics of its pupils: the percentage of English language learners (ell), the percentage eligible for subsidized meals (meals), and the percentage in their first year at the school (mobility).

gl <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals + mobility, design = dclus1)
table_regression(gl)
#> Survey-weighted linear regression: api00
#> 
#>  Variable    │    B      SE         95% CI         p   
#> ─────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │  819.28  21.39  [772.20, 866.36]  <.001 
#>  ell         │   -0.52   0.32  [ -1.23,   0.20]   .139 
#>  meals       │   -3.12   0.28  [ -3.74,  -2.51]  <.001 
#>  mobility    │   -0.17   0.44  [ -1.15,   0.81]   .711 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │  183                                    
#>  Weighted n  │ 6194                                    
#>  AIC         │ 2004.7                                  
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted linear regression. Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 11 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The coefficients, the standard errors and the p-values are those of summary(gl): table_regression() reads a design-based fit and computes none of its inference. What it adds is in the fit statistics and the note.

  • n is the number of schools in the sample. Weighted n is the sum of their design weights, the 6,194 schools of the population the estimates describe.
  • The design line of the note states what was declared, here a cluster sample of 15 PSUs with a finite population correction, and the degrees of freedom the tests of the table use.
  • Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization) names the variance estimator. Linearization “uses the linear terms of a Taylor series expansion to approximate the estimator by a linear function of the observed data” (Williams, 2008, p. 876).

On the substance, a school loses 3.1 points of API for each additional percentage point of pupils eligible for subsidized meals, with a 95% interval from 2.5 to 3.7 points. The two other coefficients are not distinguishable from zero in this sample.

Degrees of freedom come from the PSUs

The table above rests on 183 schools and tests with 11 degrees of freedom.

c(rows = nrow(apiclus1), design = degf(dclus1), model = df.residual(gl))
#>   rows design  model 
#>    183     14     11

The sample is a sample of 15 districts, and the schools of a district were taken together. Clustering “results in fewer degrees of freedom in the sense that the sample now focuses on a smaller number of sampling units, that is, the first-stage clusters” (Lavrakas, 2008, p. 787). The design has 15 PSUs in one stratum, hence 14 degrees of freedom, and survey takes the residual degrees of freedom of the model by subtraction: its help page says the rule “is correct for PSU-level covariates but is potentially very conservative for individual-level covariates” (?svyglm, survey 4.5). Three predictors leave 11.

table_regression() reads that number on the fit and never derives it: the engines of survey do not share one rule, and a Cox fit ends one degree of freedom above what the same arithmetic gives for a svyglm(). survey::regTermTest() takes the same number as the denominator of its F test.

The consequence is visible in every interval of the table. With 11 degrees of freedom the t quantile is 12% larger than the normal one:

qt(0.975, df.residual(gl)) / qnorm(0.975)
#> [1] 1.122972

A large file does not protect against this. The NHANES extract has 7,846 respondents with a cholesterol measure, drawn from 31 PSUs in 15 strata: 16 degrees of freedom for the design, and each coefficient of a model takes one of them.

Weights are not a design

lm() and glm() accept a weights argument, and passing the sampling weights there gives the right coefficients. It does not give the right inference. The same model, both ways:

lw <- lm(api00 ~ ell + meals + mobility, data = apiclus1, weights = pw)
table_regression(
  list("lm(weights = pw)" = lw, "svyglm(design)" = gl),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
#> Regression comparison: api00
#> 
#>                  lm(weights = pw)        svyglm(design)     
#>                ─────────────────────  ───────────────────── 
#>  Variable    │    B      SE      p       B      SE      p   
#> ─────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │  819.28  10.45  <.001   819.28  21.39  <.001 
#>  ell         │   -0.52   0.33   .116    -0.52   0.32   .139 
#>  meals       │   -3.12   0.21  <.001    -3.12   0.28  <.001 
#>  mobility    │   -0.17   0.39   .663    -0.17   0.44   .711 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │  183                    183                  
#>  Weighted n  │ 6194                   6194                  
#>  R²          │    0.72                    –                 
#>  Adj. R²     │    0.71                    –                 
#>  AIC         │ 2002.9                 2004.7                
#> 
#> Note. lm(weights = pw): linear regression; svyglm(design): survey-weighted linear regression. svyglm(design): Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 11 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC), not comparable with the likelihood AIC of the other models. Std. errors: lm(weights = pw): classical (OLS), svyglm(design): design-based (Taylor linearization). AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The two columns of coefficients are identical. The standard error of the intercept doubles under the design, from 10.45 to 21.39, and that of meals goes from 0.21 to 0.28. lm() treats the 183 schools as independent draws, and reads each weight as a precision. The R² row is filled for the lm() only: spicy reports no R² for a design-based fit.

The error does not always run in the same direction. A logistic model of high cholesterol on NHANES, with the weights rescaled to average 1 for glm():

fit <- svyglm(
  HI_CHOL ~ agecat + race + sex,
  design = dnh,
  family = quasibinomial
)

nh <- subset(nhanes, !is.na(HI_CHOL))
nh$w <- nh$WTMEC2YR / mean(nh$WTMEC2YR)
naive <- glm(
  HI_CHOL ~ agecat + race + sex,
  data = nh,
  family = quasibinomial,
  weights = w
)

table_regression(
  list("glm(weights = )" = naive, "svyglm(design)" = fit),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
#> Regression comparison: HI_CHOL
#> 
#>                        glm(weights = )          svyglm(design)       
#>                      ────────────────────  ───────────────────────── 
#>  Variable          │    B      SE     p         B         SE     p   
#> ───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)       │   -4.74  0.30  <.001         -4.74  0.32  <.001 
#>  agecat:           │                                                 
#>    (0,19] (ref.)   │     –     –     –              –     –     –    
#>    (19,39]         │    2.28  0.29  <.001          2.28  0.33  <.001 
#>    (39,59]         │    3.21  0.29  <.001          3.21  0.36  <.001 
#>    (59,Inf]        │    3.03  0.29  <.001          3.03  0.35  <.001 
#>  race:             │                                                 
#>    Hispanic (ref.) │     –     –     –              –     –     –    
#>    White           │   -0.08  0.11   .437         -0.08  0.08   .316 
#>    Black           │   -0.43  0.16   .007         -0.43  0.15   .019 
#>    Other           │   -0.15  0.18   .405         -0.15  0.34   .674 
#>  sex:              │                                                 
#>    Male (ref.)     │     –     –     –              –     –     –    
#>    Female          │    0.21  0.07   .004          0.21  0.08   .033 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌

AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Std. errors: glm(weights = ): classical (Fisher information), svyglm(design): design-based (Taylor linearization). AIC = Akaike information criterion.
round(SE(fit) / sqrt(diag(vcov(naive))), 2)
#>    (Intercept)  agecat(19,39]  agecat(39,59] agecat(59,Inf]      raceWhite 
#>           1.08           1.12           1.24           1.21           0.73 
#>      raceBlack      raceOther      sexFemale 
#>           0.94           1.92           1.15

The design-based standard errors range from 0.73 to 1.92 times those of the weighted glm(), and the p-values move with them: Female from .004 to .033, Black from .007 to .019, White from .437 to .316. The weighted glm() is neither conservative nor liberal, so it cannot serve as a bound. Its tests also refer to 7,838 residual degrees of freedom, where the design has 9.

Both fits use family = quasibinomial. For svyglm() this is the convention of survey: the quasi families “give the same point estimates and standard errors” as binomial and avoid a warning about non-integer numbers of successes (?svyglm).

A logistic model on NHANES 

table_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)
#> Survey-weighted logistic regression: HI_CHOL
#> 
#>  Variable          │      OR        SE       95% CI        p   
#> ───────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)       │         0.01  0.00  [ 0.00,  0.02]  <.001 
#>  agecat:           │                                           
#>    (0,19] (ref.)   │          –     –          –          –    
#>    (19,39]         │         9.77  3.20  [ 4.66, 20.48]  <.001 
#>    (39,59]         │        24.84  8.84  [11.10, 55.56]  <.001 
#>    (59,Inf]        │        20.70  7.26  [ 9.36, 45.74]  <.001 
#>  race:             │                                           
#>    Hispanic (ref.) │          –     –          –          –    
#>    White           │         0.92  0.07  [ 0.77,  1.10]   .316 
#>    Black           │         0.65  0.10  [ 0.46,  0.91]   .019 
#>    Other           │         0.86  0.29  [ 0.40,  1.85]   .674 
#>  sex:              │                                           
#>    Male (ref.)     │          –     –          –          –    
#>    Female          │         1.24  0.10  [ 1.02,  1.50]   .033 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌

#> Note. Survey-weighted logistic regression. Design: stratified (SDMVSTRA), cluster (SDMVPSU), 31 PSUs; 9 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; SE on the OR scale (delta method); CI bounds exponentiated (asymmetric). The (Intercept) row estimates the baseline odds. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

With exponentiate = TRUE the coefficients are odds ratios, the standard errors are on the odds-ratio scale by the delta method, and the intervals are the exponentiated bounds of the intervals on the log-odds scale, which is why they are not symmetric. The note says all three.

Age dominates. Compared with respondents of 19 or younger, the odds of high cholesterol are about 10 times higher between 20 and 39, and 20 to 25 times higher after 40. The intervals are wide, from 4.7 to 20.5 for the first of these odds ratios: they carry the 9 degrees of freedom of the design. Women have higher odds than men, 1.24 times, with an interval that starts at 1.02.

Average marginal effects under the design

An odds ratio of 1.24 says nothing about how many more women than men have high cholesterol. The average marginal effect answers on the probability scale.

table_regression(fit, show_columns = c("b", "ame", "ame_ci", "ame_p"))
#> Survey-weighted logistic regression: HI_CHOL
#> 
#>  Variable          │      B         AME       95% CI        p   
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)       │        -4.74                               
#>  agecat:           │                                            
#>    (0,19] (ref.)   │          –      –          –          –    
#>    (19,39]         │         2.28   0.07  [ 0.05,  0.09]  <.001 
#>    (39,59]         │         3.21   0.17  [ 0.14,  0.20]  <.001 
#>    (59,Inf]        │         3.03   0.14  [ 0.11,  0.18]  <.001 
#>  race:             │                                            
#>    Hispanic (ref.) │          –      –          –          –    
#>    White           │        -0.08  -0.01  [-0.03,  0.01]   .313 
#>    Black           │        -0.43  -0.04  [-0.07, -0.01]   .011 
#>    Other           │        -0.15  -0.01  [-0.09,  0.06]   .660 
#>  sex:              │                                            
#>    Male (ref.)     │          –      –          –          –    
#>    Female          │         0.21   0.02  [ 0.00,  0.04]   .029 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                 │      7846                                  
#>  Weighted n        │ 255345910                                  
#>  AIC               │      5166.0                                
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted logistic regression. Design: stratified (SDMVSTRA), cluster (SDMVPSU), 31 PSUs; 9 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). AME = average marginal effect; CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

At the same age group and race, the probability of high cholesterol is on average 2 percentage points higher for women than for men, with an interval from 0 to 4 points. Between 40 and 59 it is 17 points above that of the youngest group.

Two things make these effects design-based. The average is taken with the design weights, so it describes the population and not the sample. The interval uses the variance of the design and the same t reference with 9 degrees of freedom. The p-values of the two columns are close without being equal (.019 and .011 for Black): a coefficient and its average marginal effect are two different statistics.

Testing a term: Wald and Rao-Scott

race enters the model with three coefficients, and one of them, Black, has p = .019. That is not a test of race. With four groups, one comparison in three below .05 is a weak basis, and the comparison depends on the reference category. The question “does race belong in this model” is a test of the three coefficients together.

table_regression() has no term-level test column for a design-based fit. survey provides the tests:

regTermTest(fit, ~race)
#> Wald test for race
#>  in svyglm(formula = HI_CHOL ~ agecat + race + sex, design = dnh, 
#>     family = quasibinomial)
#> F =  3.105771  on  3  and  9  df: p= 0.081573
regTermTest(fit, ~race, method = "LRT")
#> Working (Rao-Scott+F) LRT for race
#>  in svyglm(formula = HI_CHOL ~ agecat + race + sex, design = dnh, 
#>     family = quasibinomial)
#> Working 2logLR =  4.144661 p= 0.27411 
#> (scale factors:  2.3 0.43 0.25 );  denominator df= 9

The first is a Wald test, F = 3.11 on 3 and 9 degrees of freedom, p = .082. The second is the Rao-Scott test: the likelihood-ratio statistic of the working model “where the observations are independent and the weights are frequency weights”, referred to a distribution that accounts for the design (?regTermTest). It gives p = .274. The two differ in size and agree on the reading: the data do not establish a difference between the groups, whatever the single row says.

The result of such a test can be reported under the table with note_add:

table_regression(
  fit,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
  note_add = "Race: Wald F(3, 9) = 3.11, p = .082."
)
#> Survey-weighted logistic regression: HI_CHOL
#> 
#>  Variable          │      OR           95% CI        p   
#> ───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)       │         0.01  [ 0.00,  0.02]  <.001 
#>  agecat:           │                                     
#>    (0,19] (ref.)   │          –          –          –    
#>    (19,39]         │         9.77  [ 4.66, 20.48]  <.001 
#>    (39,59]         │        24.84  [11.10, 55.56]  <.001 
#>    (59,Inf]        │        20.70  [ 9.36, 45.74]  <.001 
#>  race:             │                                     
#>    Hispanic (ref.) │          –          –          –    
#>    White           │         0.92  [ 0.77,  1.10]   .316 
#>    Black           │         0.65  [ 0.46,  0.91]   .019 
#>    Other           │         0.86  [ 0.40,  1.85]   .674 
#>  sex:              │

Comparing models without a likelihood

Two models side by side, with and without race:

fit0 <- svyglm(HI_CHOL ~ agecat + sex, design = dnh, family = quasibinomial)

table_regression(
  list("Age, sex" = fit0, "+ race" = fit),
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"),
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "aic", "eff_p")
)
#> Survey-weighted logistic regression comparison: HI_CHOL
#> 
#>                                    Age, sex                     + race          
#>                         ──────────────────────────────  ─────────────────────── 
#>  Variable             │   OR         95% CI        p      OR         95% CI     
#> ──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

#>  n                    │ 7846                            7846

#>                      + race 
#>                      ────── 
#>  Variable          │ p (OR) 
#> ───────────────────┼────────

#>  agecat:           │

AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; CI bounds exponentiated. The (Intercept) row estimates the baseline odds. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The AIC row of a svyglm() fit is not the AIC of a glm(). survey defines it “using the Rao-Scott approximation to the weighted loglikelihood (Lumley and Scott, 2015). It replaces the usual penalty term p […] by the trace of the generalised design effect matrix” (?anova.svyglm). show_fit_stats = "eff_p" displays that penalty as Effective parameters. Here the model with race has seven coefficients beyond the intercept and 12.9 effective parameters: under this design, a coefficient costs more than one unit.

The criterion is lower without race, 5162.1 against 5166.0, which is the reading of the two tests of the previous section. The design-based AIC compares design-based fits of the same data. It should not be set against the AIC of a glm() shown in another column.

survey also compares the two fits directly, with the same Rao-Scott test as above:

anova(fit0, fit)
#> Working (Rao-Scott+F) LRT for race
#>  in svyglm(formula = HI_CHOL ~ agecat + race + sex, design = dnh, 
#>     family = quasibinomial)
#> Working 2logLR =  4.144661 p= 0.27411 
#> (scale factors:  2.3 0.43 0.25 );  denominator df= 9

nested = TRUE, which adds the change statistics of a hierarchy to the table, is refused for a design-based fit:

table_regression(list(fit0, fit), nested = TRUE)
#> Error in `table_regression()`:
#> ! `nested = TRUE` is not available for `svyglm`.
#> ℹ The change statistics compare each model with the one before it, and this class has no test of two nested fits here. One model that cannot be compared removes the comparison for the whole table.
#> ℹ Render the models side by side with `nested = FALSE`.
#> ℹ For a design-based fit, test a term with `survey::regTermTest(fit, ~term)`. Two nested `svyglm()` or `svycoxph()` fits are compared by `anova(fit0, fit)`.

Subpopulations

An analysis of a subgroup is a domain analysis, and the subgroup is taken on the design, not on the data. “Estimates for subpopulations or domains are handled by setting to zero the observed values for all units that fall outside of the domain” (Binder, 2008, p. 192): subset() on a design does this, “keeping the original design information about number of clusters, strata” (?subset.survey.design).

older <- subset(dnh, agecat == "(59,Inf]")
fit_old <- svyglm(HI_CHOL ~ race + sex, design = older, family = quasibinomial)
table_regression(fit_old, exponentiate = TRUE)
#> Survey-weighted logistic regression: HI_CHOL
#> 
#>  Variable          │     OR        SE      95% CI       p   
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)       │        0.12  0.02  [0.08, 0.18]  <.001 
#>  race:             │                                        
#>    Hispanic (ref.) │         –     –         –         –    
#>    White           │        0.95  0.14  [0.69, 1.32]   .760 
#>    Black           │        0.73  0.21  [0.39, 1.38]   .309 
#>    Other           │        0.95  0.38  [0.40, 2.25]   .905 
#>  sex:              │                                        
#>    Male (ref.)     │         –     –         –         –    
#>    Female          │        2.31  0.42  [1.56, 3.42]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n                 │     1880                               
#>  Weighted n        │ 51225892                               
#>  AIC               │     1609.5                             
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted logistic regression. Design: stratified (SDMVSTRA), cluster (SDMVPSU), 31 PSUs; 12 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; SE on the OR scale (delta method); CI bounds exponentiated (asymmetric). The (Intercept) row estimates the baseline odds. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

Among respondents of 60 and over, the odds ratio of women is 2.31, with an interval from 1.56 to 3.42, against 1.24 in the whole sample. The n row counts the 1,880 respondents of the domain, and the note counts the PSUs that hold one of them, here all 31.

Subsetting the data first and declaring the design afterwards breaks the design. For the smallest group, the design is declared without complaint and the model stops:

other_data <- subset(nhanes, race == "Other")
d_other <- svydesign(
  id = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTMEC2YR,
  nest = TRUE, data = other_data
)
svyglm(HI_CHOL ~ sex, design = d_other, family = quasibinomial)
#> Error in `onestrat()`:
#> ! Stratum (75) has only one PSU at stage 1

One stratum has respondents of this group in a single PSU, and a variance cannot be computed from one unit. That stratum has two PSUs in the survey. Taken on the design, the same subgroup gives a model:

fit_other <- svyglm(
  HI_CHOL ~ sex,
  design = subset(dnh, race == "Other"),
  family = quasibinomial
)
table_regression(fit_other, exponentiate = TRUE, show_columns = c("b", "ci", "p"))
#> Survey-weighted logistic regression: HI_CHOL
#> 
#>  Variable      │     OR          95% CI       p   
#> ───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)   │        0.13  [0.06, 0.26]  <.001 
#>  sex:          │                                  
#>    Male (ref.) │         –         –         –    
#>    Female      │        0.75  [0.31, 1.83]   .504 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n             │      458                         
#>  Weighted n    │ 18199566                         
#>  AIC           │      301.2                       
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted logistic regression. Design: stratified (SDMVSTRA), cluster (SDMVPSU), 29 PSUs; 13 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; CI bounds exponentiated. The (Intercept) row estimates the baseline odds. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The note counts 29 PSUs, those that hold a respondent of this group with a cholesterol measure. In 15 strata they leave 14 degrees of freedom for the design, and 13 for the tests of a model with one predictor.

The error is not always that visible. For the high schools of the cluster sample, present in 8 of the 15 districts, both routes give a model, and their standard errors differ by 4%:

high_design <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals, design = subset(dclus1, stype == "H"))
high_data <- svyglm(
  api00 ~ ell + meals,
  design = svydesign(
    id = ~dnum, weights = ~pw, fpc = ~fpc,
    data = subset(apiclus1, stype == "H")
  )
)
table_regression(
  list("subset(design)" = high_design, "subset(data)" = high_data),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "p")
)
#> Survey-weighted linear regression comparison: api00
#> 
#>                   subset(design)         subset(data)     
#>                ────────────────────  ──────────────────── 
#>  Variable    │   B      SE      p      B      SE      p   
#> ─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │ 733.33  32.75  <.001  733.33  33.98  <.001 
#>  ell         │  -4.32   1.69   .051   -4.32   1.75   .057 
#>  meals       │  -1.33   1.12   .289   -1.33   1.17   .305 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │  14                    14                  
#>  Weighted n  │ 474                   474                  
#>  AIC         │ 153.1                 153.5                
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted linear regression models. Design: cluster (dnum), 8 PSUs, with finite population correction; 5 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The size of the error depends on the design, and nothing in the output of the wrong route warns of it. Subsetting the design costs nothing and is right in every case.

Replicate weights

A design can be declared by replicate weights in place of strata and clusters. “Some recent large-scale surveys specify replication weights rather than the sampling design (partly for privacy reasons)” (?svrepdesign). The functions are the same, and so are the coefficients, which depend on the weights alone. The variance is computed from the estimates obtained with each set of replicate weights.

rclus1 <- as.svrepdesign(dclus1)
gl_rep <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals + mobility, design = rclus1)

table_regression(
  list("Linearization" = gl, "Jackknife (JK1)" = gl_rep),
  show_columns = c("b", "se", "ci")
)
#> Survey-weighted linear regression comparison: api00
#> 
#>                         Linearization            Jackknife (JK1) 
#>                ────────────────────────────────  ─────────────── 
#>  Variable    │    B      SE         95% CI           B      SE   
#> ─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │  819.28  21.39  [772.20, 866.36]    819.28  22.98 
#>  ell         │   -0.52   0.32  [ -1.23,   0.20]     -0.52   0.35 
#>  meals       │   -3.12   0.28  [ -3.74,  -2.51]     -3.12   0.30 
#>  mobility    │   -0.17   0.44  [ -1.15,   0.81]     -0.17   0.54 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │  183                                183           
#>  Weighted n  │ 6194                               6194           
#>  AIC         │ 2004.7                             2007.1         
#> 
#>                Jackknife (JK1)  
#>                ──────────────── 
#>  Variable    │    95% CI (B)    
#> ─────────────┼──────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │ [768.70, 869.85] 
#>  ell         │ [ -1.29,   0.26] 
#>  meals       │ [ -3.78,  -2.47] 
#>  mobility    │ [ -1.35,   1.02] 
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted linear regression models. Linearization: Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 11 residual degrees of freedom. Jackknife (JK1): Design: replicate weights (JK1), 15 replicates; 11 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Std. errors: Linearization: design-based (Taylor linearization); Jackknife (JK1): design-based (replicate weights, JK1). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The note names the design of each model: the PSUs of the linearization, the scheme and the number of replicates of the jackknife. The jackknife and the linearization estimators “are approximately the same for point estimates for which they are valid on large samples” (Lee, 2008, p. 404). With 15 PSUs the sample of PSUs is not large, and the two differ by 7% for the intercept and by 21% for mobility.

Ordinal outcomes: svyolr()

svyolr() fits a cumulative logit model under the design. The API score cut into three bands, on the stratified sample:

apistrat$grade <- cut(
  apistrat$api00,
  c(0, 600, 700, 1000),
  labels = c("low", "mid", "high"),
  ordered_result = TRUE
)
dgrade <- svydesign(
  id = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw, data = apistrat, fpc = ~fpc
)
ol <- svyolr(grade ~ ell + meals + stype, design = dgrade)
table_regression(ol, exponentiate = TRUE)
#> Survey-weighted cumulative logit regression (proportional odds): grade
#> 
#>  Variable     │   OR      SE       95% CI         p   
#> ──────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────
#>  ell          │    0.97  0.02  [  0.94,  1.01]   .173 
#>  meals        │    0.90  0.02  [  0.87,  0.93]  <.001 
#>  stype:       │                                       
#>    E (ref.)   │     –     –           –          –    
#>    H          │    0.02  0.01  [  0.01,  0.05]  <.001 
#>    M          │    0.11  0.05  [  0.05,  0.27]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Thresholds:  │                                       
#>    low | mid  │   -8.33  0.92  [-10.15, -6.51]  <.001 
#>    mid | high │   -5.27  0.69  [ -6.63, -3.91]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n            │  200                                  
#>  Weighted n   │ 6194                                  
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted cumulative logit regression (proportional odds). Design: stratified (stype), with finite population correction; 193 residual degrees of freedom. Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; SE on the OR scale (delta method); CI bounds exponentiated (asymmetric). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Thresholds: latent-scale category cut-points (log-odds scale, not exponentiated). CI = confidence interval.

Under proportional odds one ratio applies to every cut of the scale: each additional percentage point of pupils eligible for subsidized meals multiplies the odds of a higher band by 0.90. The cut-points are in a Thresholds block, on the log-odds scale and never exponentiated, which the note states. There is no AIC row: survey has no such criterion for a svyolr() fit.

The average marginal effects of an ordinal model come one column per category of the outcome, and those of a predictor sum to zero across the categories:

table_regression(ol, show_columns = c("b", "ame"))
#> Survey-weighted cumulative logit regression (proportional odds): grade
#> 
#>  Variable     │    B     AME low  AME mid  AME high 
#> ──────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────
#>  ell          │   -0.03     0.00     0.00     -0.00 
#>  meals        │   -0.10     0.01     0.00     -0.01 
#>  stype:       │                                     
#>    E (ref.)   │     –        –        –         –   
#>    H          │   -4.12     0.33     0.03     -0.36 
#>    M          │   -2.16     0.16     0.04     -0.20 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Thresholds:  │                                     
#>    low | mid  │   -8.33                             
#>    mid | high │   -5.27                             
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n            │  200                                
#>  Weighted n   │ 6194                                
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted cumulative logit regression (proportional odds). Design: stratified (stype), with finite population correction; 193 residual degrees of freedom. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). AME of a continuous predictor: average slope (dY/dX). Thresholds: latent-scale category cut-points. AME = average marginal effect on a response-category probability.

Cox models: svycoxph()

The example of ?svycoxph, which the help page itself introduces as a “somewhat unrealistic example of nonresponse bias”: the patients of the Mayo Clinic data on primary biliary cholangitis who were randomized, weighted by the inverse of an estimated probability of being randomized.

data(pbc, package = "survival")
pbc$randomized <- with(pbc, !is.na(trt) & trt > 0)
bias <- glm(randomized ~ age * edema, data = pbc, family = binomial)
pbc$randprob <- fitted(bias)

dpbc <- svydesign(
  id = ~1, prob = ~randprob, strata = ~edema,
  data = subset(pbc, randomized)
)
cx <- svycoxph(
  survival::Surv(time, status > 0) ~ log(bili) + protime + albumin,
  design = dpbc
)
table_regression(
  cx,
  exponentiate = TRUE,
  show_fit_stats = c("nobs", "weighted_nobs", "n_events", "concordance")
)
#> Survey-weighted Cox proportional hazards regression: Surv(time, status > 0)
#> 
#>  Variable    │   HR     SE      95% CI       p   
#> ─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────
#>  log(bili)   │   2.43  0.22  [2.03, 2.90]  <.001 
#>  protime     │   1.28  0.10  [1.09, 1.50]   .003 
#>  albumin     │   0.35  0.07  [0.24, 0.53]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │ 312                               
#>  Weighted n  │ 418                               
#>  N events    │ 144                               
#>  Concordance │   0.81                            
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted Cox proportional hazards regression. Design: stratified (edema); 307 residual degrees of freedom. Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as HR; SE on the HR scale (delta method); CI bounds exponentiated (asymmetric). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). HR = hazard ratio; CI = confidence interval.

prob takes the probability, and survey inverts it: the weighted n is the 418 patients of the cohort, for 312 in the analysis. The standard errors are the design-based ones of survey, and the tests refer to a t distribution with the residual degrees of freedom of the note. A list of tokens in show_fit_stats replaces the default rows, so "weighted_nobs" has to be named to stay in the table.

What spicy refuses for survey fits, and why

A request that the design cannot honor gets an error that says why.

  • vcov =. The variance of the design is the robust variance for the declared design. To change the estimator, change the design and refit. A cluster = is ignored with a warning that says the same.
  • Statistics of a likelihood: "bic", "aicc", "deviance", "log_lik" and the pseudo-R² tokens. The exception is "aic" for svyglm(), the design-based criterion of the previous sections.
  • The AME columns of a svycoxph() model, as for any Cox model.
  • nested = TRUE and the term-level test columns. The tests exist in survey, regTermTest() and anova(), and their result can be reported with note_add.
  • standardized. Average marginal effects are the way to compare predictors on a common scale here.
  • ci_method = "profile", which needs a likelihood to profile.
  • The RMST and risk-difference columns of a Cox model. Their uncertainty comes from resampling subjects, which ignores the strata and the clusters of the design. survey::svykm() gives a marginal survival curve under the design.
  • table_regression_uv() on a design object. Fit each model with svyglm() and pass the fits to table_regression().
table_regression(fit, vcov = "HC3")
#> Error in `table_regression()`:
#> ! `vcov = "HC3"` is not available for `svyglm` models.
#> ℹ The fit's own design-based (Taylor / replicate) variance is already the robust variance for the declared design.
#> ℹ To account for clustering, declare it in the design: survey::svydesign(ids = ~cluster, ...), then refit.

The refusal of the RMST and risk-difference columns rests on a measurement. On simulated data, over five designs and three seeds, a bootstrap of the rows gave a contrast between clusters a standard error too small by a factor of 1.5 to 6, depending on the number and the size of the clusters (about 3 for 30 clusters of 25 units with a moderate intra-cluster correlation). A contrast within clusters came out about right, and so did a design without intra-cluster correlation. The ratios are the same for the Cox coefficients themselves: this is the ordinary design effect, carried onto the RMST and the risk difference.

)

Note. Survey-weighted logistic regression models. Design: stratified (SDMVSTRA), cluster (SDMVPSU), 31 PSUs; residual degrees of freedom: 12 (Age, sex), 9 (+ race). AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Coefficients exponentiated and displayed as OR; CI bounds exponentiated. The (Intercept) row estimates the baseline odds. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). CI = confidence interval; LL = lower limit; UL = upper limit; AIC = Akaike information criterion.
